summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over FDDI networks and how link-local and autoconfigured addresses are formed there. It replaces RFC 2019. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2467 defines how IPv6 packets travel over FDDI networks. It specifies the frame fields, maximum packet size, address formation and how IPv6 addresses map to FDDI hardware addresses.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets are framed, addressed and mapped to link-layer addresses on FDDI networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs rules for carrying packets over FDDI, including the frame format, MTU, interface identifier and address mapping.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses LLC/SNAP framing with Ethertype 86DD, sets a default MTU of 4352 octets and defines EUI-64-based identifiers and FDDI multicast mapping.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2467 replaces RFC 2019 and has been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2467 is a Proposed Standard published in December 1998. It obsoletes RFC 2019 and has been updated by RFC 8064.

sections.title: What the FDDI Specification Covers
sections.content:
This RFC defines the frame format for IPv6 packets on FDDI, how link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses are formed, and how link-layer address options are carried in Neighbor Discovery messages. FDDI in this document also includes CDDI.

It replaces RFC 2019. It covers how IPv6 uses this link technology rather than defining IPv6 itself.
sections.plainLanguage: This document sets the rules for carrying IPv6 across FDDI. It covers frames, addresses and Neighbor Discovery address fields.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
FDDI permits frames up to 4500 octets. After link encapsulation, a larger IPv6 packet could fit in principle, but the RFC chooses a default MTU of 4352 octets to leave room for variable MAC headers and future frame-status extensions.

A Router Advertisement can specify a smaller MTU, and a node can also be configured manually. An advertised MTU above 4352 or above the manually configured limit must otherwise be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets the default IPv6 packet size below the largest possible FDDI frame. A router or manual setting may lower that limit, but not raise it above the specified maximum.

sections.title: The FDDI Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are sent in asynchronous FDDI frames using unrestricted tokens. Nodes should also be able to receive synchronous frames and asynchronous frames using restricted tokens. Frames use LLC/SNAP encapsulation with long-format 48-bit addresses.

The frame's data field contains the IPv6 header and payload. The fixed header values include FC in the hexadecimal range 50 to 57, DSAP and SSAP set to AA, CTL set to 03, OUI set to 000000 and Ethertype set to 86DD.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reads the FDDI header values to identify the enclosed packet as IPv6. The frame uses LLC/SNAP and 48-bit link addresses.

sections.title: Bridges Between Different Media
sections.content:
A bridge may connect FDDI to another medium, such as Ethernet, but bridges do not all handle IPv6 Path MTU Discovery correctly. IPv6 communication across mixed media must not depend on bridge support unless the bridges are known to implement that function correctly.

When bridges do not support IPv6 Path MTU Discovery, routers must advertise the smallest MTU among the connected media. If no routers are present, nodes attached to media with a larger default MTU must be configured with that smaller size.
sections.plainLanguage: Every network segment along a bridged path must be able to carry the packet size in use. If a bridge cannot report a smaller limit, routers or manual settings must provide it.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Address Mapping
sections.content:
An FDDI interface identifier is derived from the built-in 48-bit MAC address by inserting the EUI-64 values and complementing the Universal/Local bit. A stateless-autoconfiguration prefix on FDDI must be 64 bits. The link-local address combines the FE80::/64 prefix with the interface identifier.

Neighbor Discovery maps unicast IPv6 addresses to the FDDI address the interface currently uses. For multicast, the FDDI address begins with hexadecimal 3333 and ends with the last four octets of the IPv6 destination.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface builds its identifier from its hardware address and combines it with the link-local prefix. Multicast mapping uses the last four address octets after the FDDI prefix 3333.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2019
sections.content: RFC 2467 removes FDDI adjacency detection, replaces the earlier 48-bit Address Token with a 64-bit Interface Identifier based on EUI-64, and changes the stateless-autoconfiguration prefix requirement to 64 bits. The link-local prefix is also 64 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision removes the old adjacency feature and uses a 64-bit interface identifier. It also specifies 64-bit prefixes for autoconfiguration and link-local addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Deriving interface identifiers from MAC addresses is intended to preserve global uniqueness when possible. The method does not prevent accidental duplication or deliberate forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: An identifier based on a hardware address can still be duplicated by mistake or forged. The derivation method does not prevent either problem.
